claim: Rising temperatures, with attendant increases in drought as well as insect and disease outbreaks, are predicted to result in net losses in yield of North American crops by the end of the 21st century.
source: Projected impacts of climate change on crop yields vary widely depending on crop type and location; however, rising temperatures, with attendant increases in drought as well as insect and disease outbreaks, are predicted to result in net losses in yield of North American crops by the end of the 21st century (Settele et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Settele et al., 2014

claim: Water stress accounts for the largest proportion of crop loss in the U.S.
source: Water stress accounts for the largest proportion of crop loss in the U.S., and an estimated 45% of U.S. land surface suffers from low water availability (DeLucia et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to DeLucia et al., 2014

claim: An estimated 45% of U.S. land surface suffers from low water availability.
source: Water stress accounts for the largest proportion of crop loss in the U.S., and an estimated 45% of U.S. land surface suffers from low water availability (DeLucia et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to DeLucia et al., 2014

claim: Plants can exhibit either drought escape or drought resistance mechanisms in response to soil water deficit.
source: In response to soil water deficit, plants can exhibit either drought escape or drought resistance mechanisms (Levitt, 1980; Harb et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Levitt, 1980 and Harb et al., 2010

claim: Under drought escape, plants complete their life cycle before the onset of stress.
source: Under drought escape, plants complete their life cycle before the onset of stress.
evidence: Draws from established scientific understanding of drought escape mechanisms

claim: Drought resistance can occur through dehydration avoidance or through tolerance.
source: Drought resistance can occur through dehydration avoidance or through tolerance (Levitt, 1980).
evidence: Supported by citation to Levitt, 1980

claim: With dehydration avoidance, plants maintain high cellular water potential by lowering stomatal conductance and/or reducing water loss through changes in leaf area or orientation and by increasing resource allocation to roots.
source: With dehydration avoidance, plants maintain high cellular water potential by lowering stomatal conductance and/or reducing water loss through changes in leaf area or orientation and by increasing resource allocation to roots.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge of dehydration avoidance mechanisms

claim: Drought tolerant plants conserve cell turgor through osmotic adjustments to survive the drought stress.
source: Drought tolerant plants conserve cell turgor through osmotic adjustments to survive the drought stress (Levitt, 1980) and may also tolerate lower cell water potentials through anisohydric water potential regulation (Franks et al., 2007) while maintaining cellular metabolism (Sade et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Levitt, 1980; Franks et al., 2007; and Sade et al., 2012

claim: Intrinsic water use efficiency (WUE) is defined as the ratio between stomatal conductance (gs) and CO2 assimilation (A).
source: A commonly used measure for assessing drought resistance is the intrinsic water use efficiency (WUE), which is defined as the ratio between stomatal conductance (gs) and CO2 assimilation (A) (Condon et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Condon et al., 2002

claim: WUE is not always an accurate predictor of yield capacity under drought.
source: WUE is often used as a proxy for drought resistance, but it is not always an accurate predictor of yield capacity under drought (Medrano et al., 2012) especially when biomass allocation to roots increases in response to drought (Edwards et al., 2016) or when yield is tightly correlated with water use (Blum, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Medrano et al., 2012; Edwards et al., 2016; and Blum, 2009

claim: Many drought-responsive genes are under circadian regulation.
source: Many drought-responsive genes are under circadian regulation (Covington et al., 2008) resulting in specific time-of-day responses to drought (Wilkins et al., 2010; Dubois et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Covington et al., 2008; Wilkins et al., 2010; and Dubois et al., 2017

claim: The genus Brassica includes the closest crop relatives of Arabidopsis.
source: The genus Brassica includes the closest crop relatives of Arabidopsis and therefore is an excellent crop model for comparative studies, including analyses of adaptive drought responses.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge of plant phylogeny

claim: Rapeseed (B. napus) is an allopolyploid derived via hybridization between B. rapa and B. oleracea.
source: Rapeseed (B. napus), an allopolyploid derived via hybridization between B. rapa and B. oleracea, is the second largest oil crop after soybean with an annual global production of 70 million tons (http://faostat.fao.org, 2014).
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge of Brassica genetics

claim: Rapeseed is the second largest oil crop after soybean with an annual global production of 70 million tons.
source: Rapeseed (B. napus), an allopolyploid derived via hybridization between B. rapa and B. oleracea, is the second largest oil crop after soybean with an annual global production of 70 million tons (http://faostat.fao.org, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to faostat.fao.org, 2014

claim: Water was completely withheld from the droughted cohort of B. rapa (Yellow Sarson) R500 beginning at 16 days after sowing (DAS).
source: We assessed the early stages of mild drought, completely withholding water for the droughted cohort of B. rapa (Yellow Sarson) R500 beginning at 16 days after sowing (DAS).
evidence: Describes the experimental procedure performed by the authors

claim: Tissue sampling and physiological measurements were conducted on Day 3 and 4 of drought, 18 and 19 DAS, respectively.
source: Tissue sampling and physiological measurements were conducted on Day 3 and 4 of drought, 18 and 19 DAS, respectively (Figure 1A, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Describes the experimental procedure and references Figure 1A

claim: After four days of drought, soil water potential (Ψs) had declined progressively to −1.5 MPa.
source: After four days of drought, soil water potential (Ψs) had declined progressively to −1.5 MPa, whereas Ψs was relatively constant between 0 and −0.5 MPa for the well-watered soil (Figure 1B, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B

claim: Soil water potential was relatively constant between 0 and −0.5 MPa for the well-watered soil.
source: After four days of drought, soil water potential (Ψs) had declined progressively to −1.5 MPa, whereas Ψs was relatively constant between 0 and −0.5 MPa for the well-watered soil (Figure 1B, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B

claim: The droughted plants showed a significant decrease in dry above-ground biomass by the end of Day 4.
source: The droughted plants showed a significant decrease in dry above-ground biomass by the end of Day 4 (Figure 2A); however, there was no wilting during the experiment (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2A

claim: There was no wilting during the experiment.
source: The droughted plants showed a significant decrease in dry above-ground biomass by the end of Day 4 (Figure 2A); however, there was no wilting during the experiment (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by visual observations shown in Figure 2B

claim: The drought conditions applied in this study capture the early perception of drought stress.
source: Therefore, the drought conditions applied in this study capture the early perception of drought stress (Harb et al., 2010).
evidence: Inferred from the experimental conditions and supported by citation to Harb et al., 2010

claim: On both Day 3 and Day 4 of drought, photosynthetic rate (A) peaked at Zeitgeber Time (ZT) five.
source: On both Day 3 and Day 4 of drought, A peaked at Zeitgeber Time (ZT) five where ZT0 corresponded to lights on (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3A

claim: At ZT5, a net CO2 uptake of 12 ± 2 μmol m−2s−1 was recorded.
source: At this time point, we recorded a net CO2 uptake of 12 ± 2 μmol m−2s−1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3A

claim: Droughted plants had photosynthetic capacity similar to well-watered plants for the duration of the experiment.
source: Droughted plants had photosynthetic capacity similar to well-watered plants for the duration of the experiment (Figure 3A), in agreement with previous studies of anisohydric plants where overall photosynthetic capacity was not disturbed by mild drought stress (Chaves et al., 2009; Cornic and Massacci, 1996; Flexas and Medrano, 2002).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3A and citations to previous studies

claim: There were significant differences in gs between droughted versus well-watered plants with a reduction of 50% late in the day (ZT13) and 30% at night (between ZT17 and ZT21) on both Day 3 and Day 4.
source: In contrast, there were significant differences in gs between droughted versus well-watered plants with a reduction of 50% late in the day (ZT13) and 30% at night (between ZT17 and ZT21) on both Day 3 and Day 4 (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3B

claim: In late afternoon and at night gs responds to small changes in soil water potential and seems to play an important role in the early response to drought.
source: Thus, in late afternoon and at night gs responds to small changes in soil water potential and seems to play an important role in the early response to drought.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing gs changes

claim: B. rapa can reduce CO2 supply before A is impacted.
source: Our results show that B. rapa, like many crops, can reduce CO2 supply before A is impacted (Edwards et al., 2016).
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data and supported by citation to Edwards et al., 2016

claim: Fv'/Fm' was significantly greater for droughted than well-watered plants on both Days 3 and 4 of drought during the middle of the light period.
source: The maintenance of photosynthetic capacity in droughted plants despite the significant decrease in gs may be partly explained by Fv'/Fm', which was significantly greater for droughted than well-watered plants on both Days 3 and 4 of drought during the middle of the light period (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3C

claim: Fv'/Fm' presented a diurnal pattern with the highest values early in the day (ZT1 and ZT5) in both droughted and well-watered plants.
source: Fv'/Fm' presented a diurnal pattern with the highest values early in the day (ZT1 and ZT5) in both droughted and well-watered plants.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3C

claim: Elevated Fv'/Fm' fully compensated for reduced gas exchange under mild drought conditions.
source: Elevated Fv'/Fm' fully compensated for reduced gas exchange under mild drought conditions.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing maintained photosynthetic capacity despite reduced gs

claim: Non-structural carbohydrates (NSC) accumulated during the day and decreased during the night in well-watered conditions.
source: As expected, non-structural carbohydrates (NSC) accumulated during the day and decreased during the night in well-watered conditions (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3D

claim: In droughted plants, NSC levels were elevated throughout the night compared to well-watered controls.
source: In droughted plants, NSC levels were elevated throughout the night compared to well-watered controls.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3D

claim: The reduction in biomass observed was not due to a reduction in carbon availability but rather to the decreased nighttime conductance that preserves leaf turgor and high water potential at the cost of sugar translocation to growing tissues.
source: The presence of above-ground NSC accumulation suggested that the reduction in biomass observed (Figure 2A) was not due to a reduction in carbon availability but rather to the decreased nighttime conductance that preserves leaf turgor and high water potential (Chaves, 1991) at the cost of sugar translocation to growing tissues (Sevanto, 2014).
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data and supported by citations to Chaves, 1991 and Sevanto, 2014

claim: Plants can lose as much as 30% of the daily water budget overnight.
source: Our findings are consistent with studies showing that plants can lose as much as 30% of the daily water budget overnight (Dawson et al., 2007; Caird et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dawson et al., 2007 and Caird et al., 2007

claim: gs is the best physiological indicator of the early perception of drought stress in the plant.
source: We found gs to be the best physiological indicator of the early perception of drought stress in the plant, consistent with the view that A and gs are regulated separately (Dodd et al., 2004; von Caemmerer et al., 2004) and that small decreases in gs do not lead directly to reductions in A under mild drought.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data and supported by citations to Dodd et al., 2004 and von Caemmerer et al., 2004

claim: The top eight modules in the network analysis contained 80–85% of the genes.
source: Not surprisingly, the top eight modules, containing 80–85% of the genes in the network analysis (see Materials and methods, Supplementary file 1), showed strong temporal expression patterns across the two-day time course (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by the network analysis results shown in Figure 4

claim: The top eight modules showed strong temporal expression patterns across the two-day time course.
source: Not surprisingly, the top eight modules, containing 80–85% of the genes in the network analysis (see Materials and methods, Supplementary file 1), showed strong temporal expression patterns across the two-day time course (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by the network analysis results shown in Figure 4

claim: Samples clustered based on time of day, rather than treatment.
source: In agreement with time-course transcriptome studies in Arabidopsis, poplar, and soybean (Wilkins et al., 2009; Wilkins et al., 2010; Rodrigues et al., 2015; Dubois et al., 2017) samples clustered based on time of day, rather than treatment, revealing that the transcriptome varied more with time of day than due to drought (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 5A and citations to previous studies

claim: The transcriptome varied more with time of day than due to drought.
source: In agreement with time-course transcriptome studies in Arabidopsis, poplar, and soybean (Wilkins et al., 2009; Wilkins et al., 2010; Rodrigues et al., 2015; Dubois et al., 2017) samples clustered based on time of day, rather than treatment, revealing that the transcriptome varied more with time of day than due to drought (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: The consensus network contained significant overlaps in module classifications between the droughted and well-watered networks.
source: The consensus network contained significant overlaps in module classifications between the droughted and well-watered networks, consistent with the strong diurnal effects on the transcriptome (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by consensus network analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: The well-watered and droughted networks contained 17 and 20 modules, respectively.
source: The well-watered and droughted networks contained 17 and 20 modules, respectively, suggesting that there are additional expression patterns in the droughted network due to rearrangement of the transcriptome in response to the drought treatment.
evidence: Supported by the network analysis results

claim: There are additional expression patterns in the droughted network due to rearrangement of the transcriptome in response to the drought treatment.
source: The well-watered and droughted networks contained 17 and 20 modules, respectively, suggesting that there are additional expression patterns in the droughted network due to rearrangement of the transcriptome in response to the drought treatment.
evidence: Inferred from the difference in module numbers between networks

claim: Roughly 95% of the genes in the wM5 module resolved into three distinct droughted modules.
source: Roughly 95% of the genes in the wM5 module resolved into three distinct droughted modules, highlighted by the different color nodes in the network view (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by network analysis shown in Figure 6B

claim: Several modules in both networks were positively or negatively correlated with various physiological measurements.
source: Several modules in both networks were positively or negatively correlated with various physiological measurements (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7A,B

claim: The wM5 and dM5 modules with peak expression between ZT1-5 were positively correlated with the A, gs, and Fv'/Fm'.
source: For example, the wM5 and dM5 modules with peak expression between ZT1-5 were positively correlated with the A, gs, and Fv'/Fm', which had similarly phased peaks (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7A,B

claim: wM7 and dM8, which peak around ZT17, were negatively correlated with A, gs, and Fv'/Fm'.
source: Conversely, wM7 and dM8, which peak around ZT17, were negatively correlated with A, gs, and Fv'/Fm'.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7A,B

claim: The dM1 module was enriched for primary metabolism and response to abiotic stimulus.
source: The dM1 module was enriched for primary metabolism and response to abiotic stimulus (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 8B,C

claim: dM5 was enriched for photosynthesis, response to light, and abiotic stress stimulus.
source: dM5 was enriched for photosynthesis, response to light, and abiotic stress stimulus (Figure 8B,C).

claim: The dM10 module with the bi-phasic peaks contained genes involved in glucosinolate biosynthesis and metabolism.
source: Interestingly, the dM10 module with the bi-phasic peaks contained genes involved in glucosinolate biosynthesis and metabolism (Figure 8B,C).

claim: Abiotic stress leads to an increase in secondary metabolism that is likely the result of carbon reallocation.
source: Previous work has shown that abiotic stress leads to an increase in secondary metabolism that is likely the result of carbon reallocation (Del Carmen Martínez-Ballesta et al., 2013).

claim: The genes in negatively correlated modules are related to photosystem efficiency and light response pathways.
source: The genes in these modules are related to photosystem efficiency and light response pathways (Figure 9B,C), consistent with the decrease in Fv'/Fm' observed on Day 4.

claim: dM7, dM11, and dM17 contain genes involved in nitrogen metabolism, amino acid biosynthesis, and phosphatase activity.
source: dM7, dM11, and dM17 show dramatic decreases in expression on Day 4 relative to well-watered plants and contain genes involved in nitrogen metabolism, amino acid biosynthesis, and phosphatase activity (Figure 9B,C).

claim: The NanoString data supported the trends observed in the RNA-seq dataset.
source: The NanoString data supported the trends observed in the RNA-seq dataset.

claim: The diel expression patterns seen in the well-watered and droughted plants and specific time-of-day responses to drought were recapitulated for the genes evaluated.
source: The diel expression patterns seen in the well-watered and droughted plants and specific time-of-day responses to drought were recapitulated for the genes evaluated (Figure 10, Figure 10—figure supplements 1 and 2, Figure 10—source data 1).

claim: COR15B and COR47 showed increased and shifted peak expression on Day 4 of droughted plants relative to well-watered plants.
source: The expression of two members of the C-repeat-binding factor (CBF) regulon COR15B and COR47 (dM1, Figure 8C) showed increased and shifted peak expression on Day 4 of droughted plants relative to well-watered plants (Figure 10) consistent with their known roles in abiotic stress response (Novillo et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by NanoString validation data shown in Figure 10 and citation to Novillo et al., 2007

claim: ELIP1/2 genes are members of chlorophyll a/b – binding (CAB) protein superfamily and postulated to be photoprotectants for PSII under various stress conditions.
source: The EARLY LIGHT-INDUCIBLE PROTEIN 1 and 2 (ELIP1/2) genes (Figure 8C), members of chlorophyll a/b – binding (CAB) protein superfamily and postulated to be photoprotectants for PSII under various stress conditions (Hayami et al., 2015) were both elevated in expression level and showed phase-delayed expression profiles (Figure 10).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hayami et al., 2015

claim: ELIP1/2 were both elevated in expression level and showed phase-delayed expression profiles.
source: The EARLY LIGHT-INDUCIBLE PROTEIN 1 and 2 (ELIP1/2) genes (Figure 8C), members of chlorophyll a/b – binding (CAB) protein superfamily and postulated to be photoprotectants for PSII under various stress conditions (Hayami et al., 2015) were both elevated in expression level and showed phase-delayed expression profiles (Figure 10).

claim: Components of PSII, LHCB2.2 and PSBY, exhibited elevated expression during the day.
source: Components of PSII, LIGHT-HARVESTING CHLOROPHYLL B-BINDING 2 (LHCB2.2) and PHOTOSYSTEM II BY (PSBY), also exhibited elevated expression during the day (Figure 8C, Figure 10).

claim: The drop in gs during the night and the accumulation of NSC in droughted plants on Day 4 of the treatment coincided with decreased expression of the gene encoding CYP79F2.
source: The drop in gs during the night and the accumulation of NSC in droughted plants on Day 4 of the treatment coincided with decreased expression of the gene encoding CYP79F2, which metabolizes long-chain aliphatic glucosinolates (Figure 8C, Figure 10).

claim: CYP79F2 metabolizes long-chain aliphatic glucosinolates.

source: Integrating these dynamic changes in physiology with the transcriptome data using a circadian-guided network approach uncovered changes in expression of several photosynthetic and metabolic genes, suggesting an early sensing of the drought treatment at the molecular level.
